data.title: Genital ulcer disease — viva
data.summary: Sexually transmitted infections · 9 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Genital ulcer disease** (Sexually transmitted infections)_

**Q1. Causes of genital ulcer disease?**
- Infective STI: syphilis, chancroid, genital herpes, LGV, donovanosis
- Non-STI: trauma, FDE, Behçet disease, aphthae, erythema multiforme/SJS, pyoderma, scabies, carcinoma (SCC), tuberculosis, pemphigus, Lipschütz ulcer (EBV in young girls)

**Q2. Describe the primary chancre of syphilis.**
- Single, painless, indurated (button-like) clean-based ulcer with raised edge, appears 9–90 days (average 21) after exposure; bilateral rubbery non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy

**Q3. Why is the incubation period of syphilis long?**
- T. pallidum has a very slow division time (~30–33 hours) and inoculum size determines the time to chancre

**Q4. Named terms DYP likes to ask?**
- Dory-flop sign: indurated chancre flips over when prepuce is retracted
- Chancre redux: relapse of chancre at original site; pseudochancre redux: gumma at site of old chancre
- Syphilis d'emblée: secondary syphilis without primary (transfusion)
- Balanitis of Follmann: syphilitic balanitis
- Condom chancre: chancre on prepuce distal to the coronal sulcus
- Phagedenic chancre: necrotic chancre with secondary infection

**Q5. Features of secondary syphilis?**
- 6–12 weeks after chancre: non-itchy symmetrical maculopapular rash including palms and soles (copper-coloured), Biett's collarette, mucous patches/snail-track ulcers, condyloma lata, split papules, moth-eaten alopecia, generalised lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms; corymbose, annular (face), lichenoid, follicular, nodular variants, lues maligna

**Q6. Investigations for syphilis?**
- Dark-ground microscopy (primary/secondary moist lesions — not oral lesions due to commensal treponemes), direct fluorescent antibody, PCR
- Non-treponemal: VDRL/RPR (quantitative, for monitoring; prozone phenomenon; biological false positives)
- Treponemal: TPHA/TPPA, FTA-ABS, CLIA/EIA (remain positive for life); reverse algorithm
- CSF VDRL (only test used on CSF) in suspected neurosyphilis

**Q7. Treatment of syphilis?**
- Early (primary, secondary, early latent): benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
- Late latent/unknown duration, tertiary (non-neuro): 2.4 MU weekly × 3
- Neurosyphilis: aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 MU/day IV × 10–14 days
- Penicillin allergy: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 14 days (28 days for late); pregnancy — desensitise and give penicillin
- Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction may occur in first 24 h

**Q8. Syndromic management (NACO)?**
- Genital ulcer non-herpetic: white kit (kit 3 — benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU + azithromycin 1 g) or blue kit (kit 4 — doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 15 days + azithromycin 1 g) if penicillin-allergic
- Herpetic ulcer: red kit (kit 5 — acyclovir 400 mg three times daily × 7 days)
- Plus counselling, condoms, partner management, HIV/syphilis testing

**Q9. Follow-up after treatment?**
- Quantitative VDRL/RPR at 3, 6, 12 (24) months — four-fold (two dilution) fall indicates adequate response; serofast state possible

## Quick spotter facts
- Single painless indurated clean ulcer with bilateral rubbery nodes — primary chancre

_Sources: DYP Survival Guide for PG Dermatology Exam (Long case — Genital ulcer/syphilis); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch.125–126; NACO STI guidelines. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
